coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 7 units (the domain directory itself plus 12.01–12.06) and 39 .md files — matches the expected 7/39 exactly. Every file was read. The corpus is ~977 KB of prose; to fit it in one context the largest sections were read through a line-truncating renderer rather than verbatim: Deep Think Annotations rows were capped (150–260 chars, preserving hypothesis + verdict + opening rationale), Cross-Cut Notes / Rejected Pairs / Cross-Cut Details / Cross-Cut Map / Decisions / Open Questions / Role Lens rows were capped at 150–420 chars, and Cross-Cut Notes + Rejected Pairs were omitted entirely for the four 12.01 feature files. Behavior, Happy Path, Edge Cases, States, Field/Condition tables and Role Matrices — where forced inventions and contradictions live — were read in full everywhere. Specific truncated cells were re-fetched verbatim where a finding turned on them (12.02 index Q-03, 12.02.03 Fan lens, 12.05 CX-03 §3, 12.05 CX-04 §3). Residual risk: a contradiction buried only in the tail of a long Deep Think outcome or a Cross-Cut Notes bullet could have been missed. Scoring: applicableCheckpoints = files-in-unit × 3, the three dimensions that genuinely apply to a vision-layer domain/feature file (3 Feature Completeness, 7 Open Question Resolution, 8 Structural Compliance), plus one checkpoint per forced-invention finding per scoring.md. Dimensions 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 are N/A throughout: problem statement, personas, constraints, success metrics and competitive landscape are owned by meta/ and are referenced, never redefined, in this domain (release-distribution-index.md:84 — 'Personas are defined in meta/personas.md — referenced only, never redefined here'). Devil's-advocate pass dropped 11 candidate findings that survived first inspection but not verification: most [PENDING — Step 5] markers in the sub-domain CX files turned out to be answered by a named downstream feature (12.01 CX-03 §3 by 12.01.04 D-04/DT-05; 12.03 CX-01 §4 by 12.03.02 D-09; 12.03 CX-04 §5 by 12.03.04 D-03; 12.02 CX-05 §5 by 12.02.02's edge-case row; 12.01 CX-02 §5 by 12.01.02's pinning table), and the apparent 12.02.03-vs-12.02.02 Fan-consequence conflict is explicitly reconciled in the parent index's resolved Q-03.

findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the domain-12 permission surface from the domain index's Role Matrix (which advertises itself as the authoritative maximum) denies the Producer any write capability in the readiness gate and in asset conformance. 12.01.03's entire design depends on the Producer clearing gate items — 'they can clear the items they are authoritative for: attaching a sample declaration, supplying the clearance doc' — and 12.01.04 names the Producer 'the authoritative persona here' and 'the only actor who can fix a real audio failure'. The gate becomes unresolvable for every release whose blocking item is a Producer-held fact.

findings.claim: 12.07 makes identifier prefix provenance three-valued (ours / the artist's / a third party's) and states that the third value is common, but 12.08's what-leaves table — the artifact that decides the exit manifest — has only two prefix rows. 12.07 names this as a live defect it owes 12.08, and no open question in either file, or at domain level, covers what a third-party-prefix identifier does on exit.
findings.evidence: 12.07-identifier-assignment-at-delivery.md:287 (D-13) — 'Prefix provenance is **three-valued** (ours / the artist's / a third party's) and recorded **per recording, never per release**'. 12.07:249 (DT-12) — '❌ REJECTED — **there is a third value, and it is common.** ... This is a live break in 12.08's model — the exit table has rows for "their prefix" and "our prefix" and no row for "someone else's", which is the row a Producer-run label produces every time.' 12.07:259 — '**Two corrections this feature owes 12.08**: its exit table needs a third row for third-party prefixes (DT-12), and its single "ISRC/UPC from our prefix" row conflates two identifiers whose exit answers differ (DT-05, Q-03).' 12.08-catalog-migration-exit.md:51-58 — the exit table contains only '| ISRC/UPC from **their** prefix | ✅ Theirs | 12.07 D-02 |' and '| ISRC/UPC from **our** prefix | ⚠️ The whole question | See DT-02 |'. 12.08 Q-01 (12.08:163) is scoped explicitly to the WeJammin-prefix case only, and domain Q-05 (release-distribution-index.md:141) is 'Scoped to **ISRC only**' on the same ours-vs-theirs axis.
findings.forcedInvention: What the export manifest says, and what leaves, for an identifier whose prefix belongs to neither WeJammin nor the departing artist — a Producer-run label's registrant prefix, or a prior distributor's on migrated catalog.
findings.failure_scenario: A departing artist's catalog contains a compilation with 14 recordings from 9 registrants (12.07's own edge case: 'Compilation of 14 recordings from 9 registrants | Correct and normal'). The exit manifest generator has two rows to match against and hits a third-party prefix on nine of them. One implementer classifies them under 'their prefix' and hands them over as the artist's; another classifies them under 'our prefix' and gates them behind the unresolved Q-01, withholding identifiers WeJammin never had any claim to.

findings.claim: A behaviour asserted twice at cross-cut level — that label copy selects which identifier prefix pool a release draws from — appears nowhere in the allocation rules of 12.07, the feature that owns assignment. 12.01's own CX file records the claim as unconfirmed with no owner and no deferral target, while the domain CX file asserts the same claim at High confidence.
findings.evidence: 12.01-release-builder-cx.md:13 (CX-04) — 'The label/band entity named in label copy determines which identifier prefix the release draws from (12.07) and which org entity owns the release | Musician | Medium | Follows from D-01 in 12.01.05 (derive from 09) plus the org-entity model in 01; **the prefix consequence needs confirming**.' Same claim at High confidence in release-distribution-cx.md:18 (CX-07) — 'Identifiers are required message fields; label copy determines which prefix pool a release draws from | Musician, Producer | High'. But 12.07's Allocation rules (12.07:80-102) never mention label copy: the only pool selection stated is 'Recordings without one are allocated an ISRC — atomically, from one registrant code and one year of reference (D-10)' (12.07:164), and 12.01.05's Field Rules table (12.01.05:45-51) has five fields — (P) line, (C) line, label name, catalog number, distributor of record — none of which is described as selecting a prefix pool.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether naming a label/band entity in label copy changes which registrant prefix 12.07 allocates from, and if so what happens when that entity holds no registrant code.
findings.failure_scenario: An artist releasing under a band entity that holds its own registrant code delivers a release. One implementer, following 12.07's allocation rules literally, allocates from WeJammin's pool and stamps provenance 'ours' — which then determines what leaves at exit (12.08). Another, following domain CX-07, allocates from the band's prefix and stamps 'a third party's'. The two produce permanently different, non-recallable identifiers and opposite exit answers for the same release.

findings.claim: `Overdue` is modelled as a first-class state in 12.02.03 and as explicitly not a state in 12.03.02. 12.03.02 flags the conflict and defers reconciliation to 'synthesis' with no owner and no stage, and 12.02.03 has not been changed — its states table still maps its `Overdue` state onto a board state that does not exist in 12.03.02's vocabulary.
findings.evidence: 12.02.03-delivery-choreography-acknowledgement.md D-01 — 'Silence is a first-class `overdue` state with an expected-response window resolved per **(partner × message type)**'; its transport states table carries '| Overdue | Window exceeded, in partner business days | `Overdue` | "Apple hasn't responded in {N} days" + what we're doing |', i.e. board state `Overdue`. Contradicted by 12.03.02-per-store-delivery-status.md, section '### `Overdue` is a qualifier, not a state (DT-15)' — '`Overdue` is **not** a member of the vocabulary above. It is a time-in-state flag the platform raises on `Sent`, `Received` or `Accepted` — because "overdue waiting for an ack" and "overdue waiting to go live" are different problems ... Collapsing them into one `Overdue` state destroys the only information that makes the row actionable.' 12.03.02's state vocabulary table lists Queued/Sent/Received/Accepted/Live (pre-order)/Live/Rejected/Withdrawn/Removed by store/Unknown — no `Overdue`. The reconciliation is deferred without an owner: 12.03.02 — '> **Reconciliation note for Step 6**: 12.02.03 D-01 lists `overdue` as a first-class *state*. This feature owns the status object (CX-02), so the refinement is made here ... 12.02.03's vocabulary and this one must be reconciled as one vocabulary during synthesis, not two.'
findings.forcedInvention: Whether the delivery status model has an `Overdue` state or an `Overdue` qualifier attached to Sent/Received/Accepted — i.e. whether the state machine has 10 states or 9 states plus a flag, and whether `Sent · overdue` and `Accepted · overdue` are distinguishable.
findings.failure_scenario: Apple has not acknowledged for 6 days. An implementer building from 12.02.03 transitions the row to `Overdue` and loses the information that the wait was for an ack rather than for a go-live; an implementer building from 12.03.02 keeps the row at `Sent` and raises a `· overdue` flag. The two produce different persisted state values for the same partner event, and 12.03.02's own escalation rules — which distinguish '`Sent · overdue` → transport/partner problem' from '`Accepted · overdue` → the domain's worst case', and which route the ack wait and the live wait to two different clocks (12.03.02 D-19) — cannot be implemented at all on top of 12.02.03's single flat state.

findings.claim: 12.02.03's transport state table declares three of its states to have 'no equivalent — gap' on the status board. One of the three (`Partially accepted`) has since been given an equivalent by a ratified decision in 12.03 and by 12.02's own CX file, so the row is now a false statement; `Held` still has no board rendering anywhere despite copy that promises the artist one.
findings.evidence: 12.02.03-delivery-choreography-acknowledgement.md states table — '| Partially accepted | Ack: `partially-accepted` (DT-07) | **no equivalent — gap** | "Apple took 11 of 12 tracks. Track 7 was refused." |', '| Failed | Transport failed after the architecture's retry policy | **no equivalent — gap** | "We couldn't reach Apple. Retrying." |', '| Held | Partner suspended, endpoint down, or our credential lapsed | **no equivalent — gap** | "Held, not lost" + honest attribution (D-06) |'. Its ack-normalisation table repeats it: '| `partially-accepted` | Release accepted, ≥1 track rejected (DT-07) | Board has no equivalent — see Cross-Cut Notes |'. Contradicted for the first case by 12.03.02 D-18 — 'Mixed DSP outcomes stay in one `(release × store × territory)` row with structured rejected-item details; the parent projects `Partial acceptance` until evidence supports a healthy full release | Owner ratification for A-05 / `r-54[1]`, 2026-07-20' and by 12.02-ddex-delivery-messaging-cx.md CX-07 — 'The parent row projects `Partial acceptance` while evidence is mixed.' `Failed` is reconciled elsewhere (12.03.02 legal transitions — 'Transport failure is not a state here — it is 12.02.03's `Failed` and stays `Sent` on the board until it resolves'), but `Held` is not: 12.03.02's vocabulary and transition table contain no `Held`, and 12.02.02's states table promises the consequence anyway — 'Artist: store unavailable in 12.03.01 **with a reason**; releases held, not failed.'
findings.forcedInvention: What the per-store status board renders while a delivery is Held because a partner profile is suspended, a partner endpoint is down, or a WeJammin credential lapsed — the release has been scheduled but not sent, and 12.02.03 promises the artist the words 'Held, not lost'.
findings.failure_scenario: Beatport's transport credentials lapse two days before a release date. 12.02.02 fans the suspension out to every queued release at once and both files promise the artist 'held, not failed' with honest attribution. The board has no state for it: one implementer leaves the rows at `Queued` (which reads as on-schedule and hides an outage that will miss the date), another moves them to `Unknown` (which 12.03.02 defines as 'we genuinely cannot tell', a false statement when we know exactly why), and a third invents a tenth state that 12.03.02's legal-transition table forbids.

findings.claim: An open question in the 12.02 index has a pipeline stage in its Owner column instead of an owner, leaving it with a deferral target and no accountable party.
findings.evidence: 12.02-ddex-delivery-messaging-index.md:75 — '| Q-02 | Which **ERN version(s)**? ERN 4.x is current; large partners still consume 3.8.2. Direct delivery means supporting both. | `/create-prd` | `/create-prd-architecture` |'. Every other question in this domain follows the documented shape — e.g. the row directly above it, '| Q-01 | Does WeJammin deliver **directly** to DSPs ... | User | ...', and 12.02.03 Q-03 '| ... | Agent | `/create-prd` |'.
findings.failure_scenario: /create-prd-architecture reaches the ERN-version decision, finds no owner named, and either takes an architecture decision that is really a commercial scoping decision (supporting both 3.8.2 and 4.x doubles the certification surface described in 12.02.02) or stalls with nobody to escalate to. Domain Q-03 already routes the direct-vs-aggregator call to the User; this question is downstream of it and loses that linkage.

findings.claim: 12.03.04 states as a decision that only verified artist IDs are emitted for delivery, while the same file's tier table says a Tier-B ID 'can be emitted and held' and its own open question asks whether Tier-B links are 'always emitted-with-warning'. The three cannot all hold.
findings.evidence: 12.03.04-artist-profile-linking-disambiguation.md D-05 — 'Links are typed **verified** (Tier-A claim/auth) vs **asserted** (Tier-B); **only verified IDs are emitted for delivery**, asserted-but-unverifiable links are flagged to Trust & Safety (24)'. Contradicted in the same file by the tier table — '| B — addressable, not claimable | Store accepts an artist ID in the ERN but has no self-serve claim/verify path | The ID **can be emitted and held**, but ownership is **asserted, not proven** — see D-05 |'. And by Q-04 — 'For a Tier-B store (addressable, not claimable), what is the acceptable evidence bar before an asserted link is treated as trusted enough to emit — **or are Tier-B links always emitted-with-warning**?' The states table scopes non-emission to Tier-A only: '| Unverified | A **Tier-A** link was asserted but not claimed | "Claim this page to use it for delivery" — not emitted until verified |'.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether an artist ID for a store that offers no claim/verify path at all is emitted in the ERN. D-05 read literally says never — which collapses Tier B into Tier C ('no ID exposed ... name-matching is the only lever') and discards the tier distinction entirely.
findings.failure_scenario: A release goes to a Tier-B store where the artist has an existing page and a stored, unverifiable ID. One implementer honours D-05 and omits the ID, so the store name-matches — which is precisely the wrong-artist-page failure the feature exists to prevent, and which 12.03.04 calls 'the one place in distribution where the first mistake is effectively permanent'. Another implementer honours the tier table and emits it. The two produce opposite outcomes on the domain's highest-consequence irreversible act.

findings.claim: 12.04.03 states as a decision that pre-saves survive a release date change. The sub-domain CX file and 12.04.01's own edge-case table both state that the pre-save grant lives at the DSP, that whether it survives is the store's behaviour rather than WeJammin's decision, and that the record can go live before a store re-points it, at which point the pre-save fires against nothing. The decision asserts a guarantee the platform is elsewhere said to be unable to make.
findings.evidence: 12.04.03-pre-save-pre-add-links.md D-04 — '| D-04 | Pre-saves survive a release date change | A date move is not the fan's fault |', restated in its edge-case table — '| Release date moves | Pre-saves must survive it | Must hold — a date move that dropped every pre-save would be catastrophic and is not the fan's fault |'. Contradicted by 12.04-release-scheduling-windows-cx.md CX-05 §1 — 'The pre-save grant lives at the DSP, not with us — we cannot re-point what we do not hold. Whether a store's pre-save survives a date change is **the store's behaviour, not our decision**, which means D-04 in 12.04.03 ("pre-saves survive a date change") may be an intent, not a guarantee'; CX-05 §2 — 'Date change → per-store pre-save re-point or re-issue → fans carried or **silently lost**. The silent-loss branch is the dangerous one, and it is invisible on both sides.' And by 12.04.01-release-date-lead-time.md's edge case — '| Date moved earlier while pre-saves exist | **The worst case in the sub-domain** (12.04 CX-05 Q5). The record can go live before a store re-points the pre-save; the pre-save fires against nothing | "Pulling this forward risks every pre-save on Spotify firing against a record that isn't there yet. We can't undo that for your fans." |'. Neither CX-05 nor 12.04.03 carries an open question on the survival guarantee; 12.04.03 Q-02 asks only whether a silently-failed pre-save is detectable.
findings.forcedInvention: What the platform actually promises the artist and the fan when a date moves: a guarantee (D-04), a per-store best-effort with disclosure of which stores carry and which drop, or a blocking warning on date moves that would orphan pre-saves.
findings.failure_scenario: An artist moves a release from 14 Aug to 21 Aug with 340 pre-saves on Spotify. An implementer building from D-04 shows the artist 'your pre-saves carry' and builds no per-store handling. Spotify does not re-point; the grants are silently lost; nobody on either side finds out, which is exactly the failure 12.04.03 DT-03 and personas.md's Fan success criterion ('never misses a release by an artist they follow') are built to prevent. An implementer building from CX-05 instead ships a per-store carried/lost breakdown and a warning on earlier moves — a materially different feature and a materially different promise.

findings.claim: The `Orphaned` state in 12.04.03 — what a fan and an artist see when a pre-saved release is cancelled or taken down — has an unresolved marker in the User-Sees column pointing at a pipeline stage that has already run, with no owner named.
findings.evidence: 12.04.03-pre-save-pre-add-links.md states table — '| Orphaned | Release cancelled | `[PENDING — Step 5]` |', and its edge-case table — '| Release is cancelled or taken down | Pre-saves are orphaned; fans authorised something that will not happen | `[PENDING — Step 5]` — the permission must still be dropped |'. Step 5 has completed across this tree: 12.01-release-builder-index.md Q-02 is marked '✅ `/ideate-discover` Step 5', and release-distribution-index.md Q-04 records that 'MoSCoW and `/ideate-validate` both ran'. Neither 12.04.03's Q-01/Q-02/Q-03 nor the sub-domain index's Q-01/Q-02/Q-03 covers it. Only the grant-drop half is answered by cross-reference: 12.05.01-voluntary-takedown.md — '| Takedown during a pre-save window | Fans authorised something that will not happen | Orphaned pre-saves (12.04.03); the grant must still be dropped |'.
findings.failure_scenario: A release with live pre-saves is taken down. Domain 12 tells the implementer to drop the OAuth grant but nothing about what either party is shown. One implementer says nothing to the fan — which per D-11 ('fans are first-class users, not CRM records') and D-02 ('the OAuth scope is stated plainly, used once, and dropped') is exactly the silent harvesting posture the feature was written against. Another notifies the fan directly, which 12.04 CX-05 §4 argues is a breach of the artist relationship ('it is the artist's news to break, not ours'). No stage owns the choice because the one it was deferred to has already run.

findings.claim: The Producer holds Config on metadata updates and Read-only on takedown, but 12.05.02 specifies that an update decomposes into takedown + redelivery on some stores. The sub-domain CX names the consequence — the Producer can effect a removal they have no permission to request — calls it 'a real hole', and no file resolves it, tracks it, or assigns it an owner.
findings.evidence: 12.05-catalog-lifecycle-after-release-cx.md CX-03 §3 (line 64) — 'Same actors, but note the asymmetry — a Producer has `Config` on updates and `Read-only` on takedown. If their update silently decomposes into a takedown on some store, they have effected a removal they had no permission to request. **That is a real hole and it follows directly from the shared machinery.**' The permissions: 12.05-catalog-lifecycle-after-release-index.md:38-39 — '| 12.05.01 Voluntary Takedown | ✅ Full | 👁️ Read-only | ❌ None | ❌ None |' and '| 12.05.02 Metadata Update & Redelivery | ✅ Full | ⚙️ Config | ❌ None | ❌ None |'. The decomposition: 12.05.02-metadata-update-redelivery.md Behavior phase 1 — 'resolves that class to one of three outcomes: *in-place* ... , *redeliver* (takedown + re-upload, losing accumulated position/streams), or *refused*'; phase 2 — 'The artist sees the split outcome per store and confirms knowing exactly what they trade.' 12.05.02's Role Lens gives the Producer 'asset-driven updates: a corrected master, a fixed mix' — and 12.01.04 DT-09/D-10 establish that a replaced master is precisely the change class that forces takedown + new ISRC. No open question in 12.05.02 (Q-01, Q-02), 12.05.01 (Q-01, Q-02, Q-03), 12.05.03 (Q-01, Q-02, Q-03) or the sub-domain index (Q-01, Q-02, Q-03) covers it.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether a Producer's Config permission on updates extends to an update that classifies as *redeliver* on one or more stores — i.e. whether the confirm step is blocked for them, escalated to the release owner, or allowed to proceed.
findings.failure_scenario: A Producer replaces a master to fix a mix fault on a live release. On Apple the change class resolves to *redeliver* — takedown plus re-upload, forfeiting stream count, playlist position and the original release date (12.01.04 D-10, 12.05.01's asymmetry table). One implementer lets them confirm, and a Read-only-on-takedown actor has just destroyed the release's accumulated history on that store without the owner's involvement. Another blocks it and the release becomes unfixable by the only person who can fix it, reproducing the failure 12.01.04 D-04 was written to eliminate.

findings.claim: 12.05.01's edge-case table still carries an ownerless, elapsed-stage unresolved marker for the fan-purchase case that the same file's own open-questions table records as resolved, with a definite answer sourced from domain 20.
findings.evidence: 12.05.01-voluntary-takedown.md edge-case table — '| Fans bought it (domain 20) | Purchase and store presence are different things | `[PENDING — Step 5]` — a fan who paid should not lose what they bought |'. Same file, Open Questions — '| Q-03 | ~~What happens to fans who **bought** it via domain 20? Store presence and a completed purchase are different things, and taking away something a fan paid for would be indefensible.~~ **Resolved — nothing happens. A takedown ends store presence and never touches a completed purchase.**' The parent index carries the same resolution and notes the drift: 12.05-catalog-lifecycle-after-release-index.md Q-03 — '**The premise has narrowed since this was written: a purchase does not vanish.** [20.06.03] D-03 — "Entitlements survive delisting"'. The unqualified claim also survives in two Role/Matrix notes: 12.05.01 Role Lens, Fan — 'The Fan experiences it as the record silently vanishing from their library'; index note — 'they are the party who most visibly experiences a takedown — the record vanishes from their library'.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer working the edge-case table (the canonical source for takedown behaviour) sees an unresolved marker pointing at a stage that has already run, with no owner to ask, and either defers the purchased-entitlement case out of scope or revokes entitlements on takedown — directly violating 20.06.03 D-03 and the resolution recorded two tables below in the same file.

findings.claim: Fingerprint registration hard-blocks a cover version registered as an original, but the adjacent live-recording-of-a-cover case carries an ownerless unresolved marker pointing at a stage that has already run — leaving the block/allow decision on a class of recording that is common in the persona's catalog undetermined.
findings.evidence: 12.06.01-fingerprint-registration.md edge-case table — '| Cover version registered as an original | Claims the composition owner's rights | Blocked; routes to 11 |' immediately followed by '| Live recording of a covered song | Same problem, harder to detect | `[PENDING — Step 5]` |'. Step 5 has completed (12.01-release-builder-index.md Q-02 — '✅ `/ideate-discover` Step 5'; release-distribution-index.md Q-04 — 'MoSCoW and `/ideate-validate` both ran'). Neither 12.06.01's Q-01/Q-02 nor the sub-domain index's Q-02/Q-03 covers it. The stakes are set by the feature's own framing: 12.06.01 D-01 — 'Registration is gated **harder than delivery**, with no override', and release-distribution-cx.md CX-09 — 'a wrong delivery embarrasses; a wrong registration deputises a machine to accuse strangers automatically, forever'.
findings.forcedInvention: Whether fingerprint registration is blocked, allowed, or allowed-with-a-declaration for a live recording that contains a covered composition — and, given D-01 admits no override, whether an artist with a live album containing covers can register any of it.
findings.failure_scenario: A musician registers a live album containing two covers. One implementer applies the sibling row's rule and hard-blocks with no override (D-01), making an entire legitimate live catalog permanently unregisterable and forfeiting its UGC revenue. Another allows it, and the fingerprint begins asserting 100% ownership of a recording of someone else's composition — the machine-scale accusation of strangers that CX-09 identifies as the one gate in domain 12 that must be unambiguously hard.
